questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a budget?
options: A financial plan for a future period, expressed in money or units
A statement of what a business actually spent last year
A forecast of the share price at the end of the year
A record of cash received and paid during a period
questions.why: A budget is forward looking, which is what distinguishes it from the historical financial statements.
whyNot: That is historical information, not a budget.
Share price forecasting is not part of budgeting.
That is a cash flow statement, which is historical.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines the principal budget factor?
options: The factor that limits activity and therefore determines which budget is prepared first
The largest single cost in the budget
The department with the biggest budget allocation
The manager responsible for approving the budget
questions.why: It is usually sales demand, but a scarce material or full capacity can take its place.
whyNot: Size of cost does not determine the order of preparation.
Budget size is not the same as the limiting factor.
That is a role within the budget committee.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a flexible budget?
options: A budget restated for the level of activity actually achieved
A budget that managers may change whenever they wish
A budget prepared for several different departments
A budget that excludes all fixed costs
questions.why: Flexing makes the comparison with actual results fair, because variable costs should differ when output differs.
whyNot: Flexing is a technical restatement, not permission to alter targets.
Covering several departments does not make a budget flexible.
Fixed costs are included; they are simply not flexed.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT included in a cash budget?
options: Depreciation
Wages paid
Payments for new equipment
Cash received from customers
questions.why: Depreciation involves no movement of cash, so it never appears in a cash budget.
whyNot: Wages are a cash payment in the month paid.
Capital payments appear in full in the month of payment.
Receipts from customers are the main inflow.

questions.stem: Sales are expected to be 24,000 units. Opening finished goods inventory is 2,000 units and closing is to be 3,500 units. What is the production budget?
options: 25,500 units
22,500 units
24,000 units
29,500 units
questions.why: Production = 24,000 + 3,500 - 2,000 = 25,500 units. Building inventory means producing more than you sell.
whyNot: That reverses the inventory adjustment.
That ignores the change in inventory.
That adds both inventory figures instead of netting them.

questions.stem: Production requires 102,000 kg of material. Opening material inventory is 9,000 kg and closing is to be 12,000 kg. What is the purchases budget in kg?
whyNot: That reverses the inventory adjustment.
That ignores the change in inventory.
That adds both inventory figures.

questions.stem: January sales are $80,000. 30% is for cash and 70% is received the following month. What is received in January from January sales?
questions.why: Only the cash proportion is received in the month of sale: 80,000 x 30% = $24,000.
whyNot: That is the credit portion, received in February.
The whole amount is not received in January.
The cash sales are received immediately.

questions.stem: December sales were $70,000 and 70% is received the month after sale. How much of this appears in January receipts?
questions.why: 70,000 x 70% = $49,000 received in January. Forgetting the opening receivables is a common error.
whyNot: That is the 30% received in December.
Only the credit portion is received in January.
That applies the wrong percentage.

questions.stem: Overheads are $9,000 a month including $2,000 of depreciation. What appears in the cash budget?
questions.why: Only the cash element is included, so the depreciation is removed: 9,000 - 2,000 = $7,000.
whyNot: That wrongly includes the depreciation.
That is the depreciation, which is excluded.
That adds the depreciation instead of removing it.

questions.stem: Opening cash is $12,000, receipts are $73,000 and payments are $69,000. What is the closing balance?
questions.why: 12,000 + 73,000 - 69,000 = $16,000, which becomes next month's opening balance.
whyNot: That omits the opening balance.
That adds all three figures.
That uses an incorrect calculation.

questions.stem: A budget set for 10,000 units shows variable costs of $6.00 per unit. What is the flexed variable cost at 12,000 units?
questions.why: Variable costs are flexed in proportion to activity: 12,000 x 6.00 = $72,000.
whyNot: That is the original budget at 10,000 units, which would not be a fair comparison.
That is the cost per unit, not the flexed total.
That doubles the output level in error.

questions.stem: Budgeted maintenance is $18,000 at 10,000 units, of which $8,000 is fixed. What is the flexed figure at 12,000 units?
questions.why: Variable element = 10,000 over 10,000 units = $1.00 per unit. Flexed = 8,000 + (12,000 x 1.00) = $20,000.
whyNot: That flexes the whole cost including the fixed part.
That fails to flex the variable element at all.
That treats the entire cost as variable and flexes it wrongly.

questions.stem: Why is comparing actual costs at 12,000 units with a budget set for 10,000 units misleading?
options: Variable costs should have been higher, so most of the variance simply reflects the higher volume
Fixed costs should have been higher, which the budget ignores
The comparison overstates the actual costs
Actual costs cannot be measured at a different activity level
questions.why: Without flexing, the variance measures volume rather than cost control, which is the whole reason flexible budgets exist.
whyNot: Fixed costs should not change with volume, which is why they are not flexed.
The actual costs are what they are; it is the benchmark that is wrong.
Actual costs are measured normally; the issue is the comparison.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines budgetary slack?
options: Deliberately understating revenue or overstating costs so the target is easier to meet
The unspent balance of a budget at the end of a period
The time allowed between preparing and approving a budget
The difference between the budget and the actual result
questions.why: Slack is an argument against pure participation, because managers judged against a budget have an incentive to make it easy.
whyNot: An unspent balance is an underspend, not slack.
That is simply part of the budget timetable.
That is a variance.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a strong argument for participative budgeting?
options: The managers closest to the work know the most, so accuracy and commitment both improve
It removes the need for a budget committee
It guarantees that no variances will arise
It makes budgets cheaper to prepare
questions.why: Participation improves both accuracy and motivation, and the usual answer combines it with independent review to control slack.
whyNot: A committee is still needed to coordinate and to review for slack.
Variances arise whatever the process.
Participation generally takes more time, not less.

questions.stem: A company's sales budget is rising every month while its cash budget worsens every month. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Growth consumes cash, because payments for materials fall due before the sales receipts arrive
The company must be making a loss on every sale
The sales budget must have been calculated incorrectly
Depreciation has been omitted from the cash budget
questions.why: Growth requires inventory and gives customers credit, so cash goes out ahead of coming in. This is a timing problem, not a profitability problem.
whyNot: Rising sales with a cash deficit is entirely consistent with profitable trading.
The pattern is normal for a growing business.
Depreciation is correctly omitted from a cash budget.

questions.stem: A cash budget shows a deficit in month three caused by buying equipment outright. What is the most appropriate remedy?
options: Finance the equipment over its life with a loan or lease
Reduce the selling price to increase sales volume
Stop charging depreciation on the equipment
Delay paying wages until the following month
questions.why: Long-term assets should be funded by long-term finance, which spreads the payment over the period the asset earns.
whyNot: A price cut reduces cash received per unit and may worsen the position.
Depreciation does not appear in a cash budget, so it has no effect.
Deferring wages is neither lawful nor practical and would damage morale.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a purpose of budgeting?
options: Coordinating departments so that production matches expected sales
Guaranteeing that the forecast will be accurate
Removing the need for management judgement
Replacing the published financial statements
questions.why: Coordination is one of the main purposes, alongside planning, communication, motivation, control and authorisation.
whyNot: A budget cannot make a forecast accurate; it rests on one.
Budgets require a great deal of judgement.
Budgets are internal; the published statements are separate and historical.

questions.stem: Why can an imposed and unattainable budget target reduce performance?
options: Staff stop trying once the target is seen as impossible
It breaches accounting standards
It makes variance analysis impossible
It reduces the fixed costs of the business
questions.why: A target that is challenging and achievable raises effort; one that cannot be met destroys it.
whyNot: Internal budgets are not governed by accounting standards.
Variances can still be calculated, but they lose their motivational value.
Target setting does not change the level of fixed costs.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes dysfunctional behaviour caused by budgeting?
options: Spending the remainder of a budget in the final month to protect next year's allocation
Preparing the sales budget before the production budget
Flexing variable costs when comparing with actual results
Involving departmental managers in setting their own budgets
questions.why: Behaviour that serves the budget rather than the business is a real cost of budgetary control, as is cutting maintenance to hit a cost target.
whyNot: That is the correct order of preparation.
Flexing is good practice.
Participation is generally beneficial, though it invites slack.

questions.stem: Which budget is prepared last?
options: The master budget
The sales budget
The cash budget
The production budget
questions.why: The master budget is the budgeted statement of comprehensive income and statement of financial position, which summarise all the others.
whyNot: The sales budget is normally first.
The cash budget is near the end but feeds into the master budget.
Production follows sales, near the beginning.
